Kashish called the next morning. "Is the discount still there?"
"Yes, madam, till month end."

passage:
Last spring I nearly paid a token amount for a one-room flat in Baner within twenty minutes of seeing it.
The broker, Eshaan, kept checking his phone. "Three more parties are coming at four. Give the token now and it's yours."
My stomach dropped at the idea of losing it. The flat had a balcony. My old place had a wall for a view.
But I said I'd sleep on it and asked him to send the rent agreement draft by email. He didn't like that.
That night I read it twice. The deposit clause was different from what he'd said out loud. On Saturday I saw two other flats, one smaller but with clear terms.
On Monday Eshaan called. "Still available, if you're interested."
I went with the smaller one. I miss that balcony sometimes. I don't miss the knot in my stomach.
Kashish

qa.q: When did Eshaan say three more parties were coming?
qa.a: Eshaan said three more parties were coming at four.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when told about the other parties?
qa.a: Kashish felt a sudden fear of losing the flat; "my stomach dropped" shows the pressure hit hard.

qa.q: Which step revealed the problem with the first flat?
qa.a: Asking for the rent agreement draft by email and reading it overnight showed the deposit clause differed from what Eshaan had said aloud.

qa.q: What does Eshaan's Monday call show about the "three more parties"?
qa.a: The flat was still available days later, so the rush was pressure rather than a real queue, and Eshaan still hoped to close the deal.

Office manager's note, Tuesday
Suraj, our admin executive, met the vendor Vishal today about the printer lease. I sat in for the first part only.
Vishal was pleasant and quick: "This rate is only for signing today. Everyone is switching." Suraj smiled and said, "Thanks. Please email the full terms and the maintenance clause. I'll reply by Thursday." Vishal pushed twice more. Suraj repeated the same words, politely, and walked him to the door.
Wednesday, Suraj put two other quotes next to Vishal's written terms and found a yearly "service fee" that was never mentioned aloud.
Thursday, Vishal called to say the "today" rate was still available. Suraj thanked him, declined, and chose another vendor.
What I did next: I asked Suraj to write up these steps so the whole office can use them for every purchase.

qa.a: Asking for the full terms by email, taking until Thursday, comparing two other quotes, and walking away from the pressure.

Saturday night
The broker showed us the Koramangala flat at noon. Nice balcony, noisy road. "Three parties are coming at four. Pay the token now and it's yours."
Tanuja squeezed my arm, which in Tanuja language means "don't". I said we'd decide tomorrow and asked for the rental agreement draft on email. The broker sighed very loudly.
Evening: we read the draft on the bed with chai. Clause 9: the deposit comes back "at owner's discretion". My stomach dropped. That was nowhere in what the broker had said.
We also went back to the two flats on 5th Cross. One is smaller, but its owner sent a clear agreement without being asked.
Tomorrow I'll message the broker that we're passing. If the flat is gone, fine. The right one won't vanish because I read something first.
Jahnavi

passage: At the tractor dealer's tent at the Sonpur fair, the salesman slid a form across the table. "Only for fair days, Yogesh-bhai. Sign today and the rotavator comes free." Yogesh turned the pen over in his fingers. The man was friendly and the machine was shiny, but half the terms were printed so small he'd need Usha's reading glasses. "Give me all the terms in writing," he said. "I'll come back tomorrow." The salesman's smile thinned. "Tomorrow maybe the offer is gone." "Then it wasn't much of an offer." That night, under the lantern, Usha read every line aloud. The interest was higher than he'd been told, and the free rotavator had a charge buried on page three. Next morning they went to the cooperative society office and to another dealer at the far end of the fair, and compared. Yogesh walked past the first tent without stopping. The salesman called out a new, lower price. Yogesh just waved.
